topic: Mojo Is Now Open Source: What Developers Should Know
summary: Modular open-sourced the complete Mojo compiler and toolchain under Apache 2.0 with LLVM Exceptions on 2026-08-18 at ModCon, one week after Mojo hit 1.0 (2026-08-11). The compiler (internal name KGEN, C++/MLIR) landed as PR #6904: 10,000 commits, 561,408 added lines, 2,853 files, zero deletions, PR body ':)' . Mojo 1.1 / MAX 26.6 (2026-09-17) then opened compiler contributions (bug fixes only) and migrated internal issues to public GitHub. MAX, the inference engine, is still source-available under the Modular Community License, so 'Mojo is open source' is a claim about the language, not the platform. Modular was acquired by Qualcomm, completed 2026-07-29 (~$3.92B announced 2026-06-24).

key_points: Component-by-component before/after table: stdlib open since 2024, MAX kernels since 2025, compiler was the last closed piece
Stresses the license split: Mojo = Apache 2.0; MAX = Modular Community License (source-available, not OSS)
Mojo as Python-superset syntax that AOT-compiles to native, with opt-in structs, SIMD, ownership
Practical build path: git clone modular/modular; ./bazelw run --config=build-mojo KGEN:mojo -- run hello.mojo
Prebuilt nightly binaries remain for devs who do not modify the compiler
Notes compiler contributions were NOT yet accepted at release (aimed end of 2026 at the time)
PR #6904 detail: 10,000 commits, 561,408 additions, 2,853 files, zero deletions, description ':' )'
KGEN = 'kernel generator' means Mojo; parser, optimization passes, MLIR dialects, debugger, mojo/kgen/kgen-opt/kgen-translate tools
Open source != open contribution at launch; HN thread litigated 'source-available vs open source' and settled in Modular's favor
Timeline table of the three waves (stdlib 2024, kernels 2025, compiler 2026) plus Mojo 1.0 semver and six-week cadence
Detailed Apache 2.0 + LLVM Exceptions reading: Section 4(a)(b)(d) waived for embedded object code; GPLv2 combination carve-out; trademark not granted
Warning that sources older than 2026-08-18 still describe the compiler as closed
'Open source vs open governance are two different things': Apache 2.0 gives a right to exit (fork), not a vote on direction
MAX is the commercial asset (graph compiler, runtime, serving) and is not Apache 2.0
Lattner philosophy: the 'soul' of a language comes from a small tight-knit design team, not a committee
Frames it as a pivoted promise: released 39 months after the May 2023 open-source pledge, and no longer promising to be a Python superset
Uses Simon Willison's reading: Python-inspired syntax tuned for GPU programming, not full Python compatibility
Release-day HN argument summary and the 'SQLite-style no-upstream model' counterpoint
Acquisition framing: all-stock Qualcomm deal announced 2026-06-24 (~$3.92B), closed end of July; 1.0 the next week; compiler open a week after that
'Accepting contributions is not required to be open source' - SQLite counter-example; 1,100+ outside stdlib PRs since 2024
Sharpest angle for kernel authors: customizing MAX kernels still requires a prebuilt Mojo compiler binary, not one built from source
Trainium / Google TPU / Qualcomm Cloud AI 100 Ultra / Dragonfly are supported but still moving into production
Apache 2.0 + LLVM Exceptions chosen so binaries compiled from Mojo carry no toolchain attribution obligations
Benchmark honesty: Mandelbrot naive port ~150x vs Python; the famous 35,000x compares hand-vectorized parallel Mojo against single-threaded vanilla CPython
On some matrix operations Mojo beats NumPy ~1.9x
Independent verification of the release date and Apache 2 license
Notes the goal changed around Aug 2025: Mojo may or may not evolve into a full Python superset, and that is acceptable
Independent confirmation that Mojo 1.1 (2026-09-17) is when community contributions to the compiler actually opened
MAX 26.6 added audio generation (MiniMax-Music3) and AMD/NVIDIA kernel speedups

stats.fact: Mojo compiler + toolchain released open source under Apache License 2.0 with LLVM Exceptions on 2026-08-18
Open-sourcing PR #6904 'Open source Mojo': 10,000 commits, 561,408 additions, 2,853 changed files, 0 deletions, merged 2026-08-18T13:29:35Z, body is ':)'
Mojo 1.0 (source stability) shipped 2026-08-11 as part of MAX/Mojo 26.5; the compiler was still proprietary that day
Mojo 1.1 / MAX 26.6 released 2026-09-17 and began accepting external compiler contributions (bug fixes only); internal issues migrated to public GitHub
Contribution areas doc: the compiler team accepts bug fixes only (diagnostics, crashes, mis-compiles with user-observable effect); no IR/pipeline/semantics changes
License split: repo LICENSE = Apache 2.0 with LLVM Exceptions; MAX usage and distribution = Modular Community License
modular/modular repo: 29,909 stars, 3,190 forks, 1,163 open issues, primary language Mojo (checked 2026-10-01)
Qualcomm completed its acquisition of Modular on 2026-07-29; Mojo, MAX and Modular Cloud continue as products and brands
Qualcomm's all-stock acquisition of Modular was announced 2026-06-24, valued around $3.92B
Since the stdlib opened in 2024, nearly 200 contributors landed 1,100+ pull requests changing 200,000+ lines of code

ModCon 2026 also announced: Modular Cloud GA (serving billions of tokens/min; flagship customer MiniMax), platform support for AWS Trainium, Google TPUs, Qualcomm Cloud AI 100 and Dragonfly, and upcoming native Windows support for Mojo
Benchmark reality check: 35,000x is hand-vectorized+parallel Mojo vs single-threaded vanilla CPython on Mandelbrot; a naive same-structure port is ~150x, and a JSON pipeline workload is ~4.1x

Modular AI agent skills for Mojo are installed with `npx skills add modular/skills`; docs offer .md versions and llms.txt for AI tooling

angles: What actually changed on 2026-08-18: the compiler was the last closed piece after stdlib (2024) and MAX kernels (2025) - show the three-wave timeline
License map that decides engineering choices: Mojo = Apache 2.0 + LLVM Exceptions (fork, retarget, ship binaries freely); MAX = Modular Community License (source-available). Do not conflate them
'Open source' is not 'open governance': Apache 2.0 gives you a right to fork, not a vote. Modular runs a small design team deliberately (Lattner's stated philosophy), Swift-style early playbook
Freshness trap for readers: most articles and even the Wikipedia article still call the compiler proprietary - everything before 2026-08-18 is stale

The contribution rules changed once already: frozen at launch (Aug 18) then opened to bug fixes only in 1.1 (Sept 17) - check contribution-areas before writing a PR, semantics/pipeline changes are rejected
Practical gotcha for kernel authors: customizing MAX kernels or models still requires a prebuilt Mojo compiler binary - building the compiler from source does not remove every dependency

Qualcomm ownership context: a chip vendor bought the language and open-sourced it a few weeks later; read it through complement commoditization and the heterogeneous-silicon strategy (CUDA alternative)

Benchmark honesty: separate the 35,000x headline (vectorized parallel Mojo vs single-threaded CPython) from the realistic 4x-150x range, and explain the zero-speedup trap when calling CPython libraries
Python compatibility pivot: no longer promising to be a Python superset - position it as a Python-inspired, GPU-first systems language, which changes the migration story

What to actually try first: Bazel source build vs --config=prebuilt-mojo, the LSP/editor tooling, Mojo agent skills for AI coding assistants, and the community libraries (Lightbug HTTP, EmberJSON, Kelvin, NuMojo)
What to watch next: whether outside compiler PRs get merged, the ecosystem alliance program (end of 2026), and native Windows support
Migration reality: Mojo calls Python and C (ffi, @export, abi('C')), so the pragmatic path is rewriting hot paths in Mojo rather than porting whole projects

notes_for_writer: Do not repeat the launch-day 'compiler PRs are frozen' framing as current: Mojo 1.1 (2026-09-17) opened compiler contributions to bug fixes. Note the docs page at mojolang.org/community/contributing/compiler/ is stale ('As of September, 2026, we're not accepting contributions') and contradicts contribution-areas.md - recommend readers check contribution-areas for the live policy.
Always separate Mojo (Apache 2.0) from MAX (Modular Community License) when using the word 'open source'.
Cite the ModCon acquisition date (2026-07-29 completed) alongside the open-source date so the sequencing is clear.
Verify exact install commands against docs.modular.com at write time - the build command and nightly version pin change frequently.
